messages.author: 2ef0caabe03f2f6c
messages.subject: Overestimation of density
parts:
I am currently using the Distance software to fit my point count data to
estimate several songbird densities and have some concerns regarding my
chestnut-backed chickadee density estimate. The density estimate I obtain
using the best model is 4.5 birds/ha which is close to being 5x larger than
the density estimates for other birds I detected as well as much larger than
densities of chickadees from another study in the same national park. I'm
afraid that I am grossly overestimating their densities and I am hoping to
find a way to fix this problem.
I've already right truncated the largest 5% of the distance detections and
I've read that left-truncating would only worsen the problem. When looking
at the frequencies of distances, I do notice that there is no shoulder and
that my highest number of detections occur at 20m, thus suggesting evasive
movement, but I've read evasive movement would cause underestimation of
density and not overestimation.

Has anyone experienced this or have suggestions for dealing with this issue?

Thanks,
Carly Gelarden
MS Candidate
Environmental Science
Western Washington University
CarlyGel...@msn.com

messages.author: 3bbe9e00c88a70b2
messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of density
parts:
Carly,

The first question that came to my mind is what is the reason
for getting density estimates 5x larger than other species.
Is it because you saw 5x more birds of this species or
because you estimate a very low detection probability?

If you saw 5x more birds (i.e., raw counts were much greater)
then it may not be how you are estimating the detection fct
but that you simply detected more birds. If your raw counts
are similar then the issue is with your detection function.

You don't provide enough information in your email to assess
what might be the problem with your det fct estimation. For
example,what proportion of birds are you estimating you
detected, and what model are you fitting? If you used a neg
exponential fct it might the cause of your problems.

Regards,

Duane Diefenbach

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of density
parts:
Adding to Duane's comments, the hazard-rate model can also fit very
spiked, implausible detection functions. For point transect data, you
often need to truncate more than 5% of the data - we suggest 10% in the
2001 book, but any cookbook rule is going to go wrong for many data
sets. Again for point transect data, your highest frequency of
detections SHOULDN'T be at zero. You can't judge whether there is a
shoulder to the detection function by looking at the frequencies of
detections (unlike for line transect sampling). That is why Distance
produces two plots for each analysis - one corresponding to frequencies
of detections (the 'probability density function'), and the other of
scaled frequencies, with the fitted detection function. The latter plot
allows you to assess whether there is a shoulder.

Steve Buckland
